# 1. Introduction

- Provide a brief overview of your dataset

- Explain the purpose of the analysis.

- Describe outcome variable + relevant predictors as statistical types.

- This can be taken from your Phase 1 report.

- State your hypothesis for Task 1 (three predictors, must include a differential effect)

- If completing a comparison model, state your hypothesis for Task 3.

# 2. Methods
Follow the approaches and reporting conventions used in the module and required in the CA Phase 2 rubric.


- Provide a concise methodology overview.
- State your cut-off value (typically p < .05 unless otherwise specified).

## 2.1 Univariate Exploration

- Describe the approach used to examine variables of different types
  - Assessment of continuous variables

    - Heuristic normality checks + appropriate summary statistics based on assessment
    
    - Identify outliers prior to modelling

    - Visualisations: histograms, density plots, boxplots

  -  Assessment of categorical variables

    - Frequencies and proportions

    - Visualisations: barplots

  - Missingness checks

    - Patterns of missing data

    - Decisions regarding exclusion or imputation (if relevant)

  - Notes on variable suitability

    - Any issues identified that may require transformation/adjustment

## 2.2 Bivariate Exploration

- Describe bivariate tests/visuals used to justify predictor inclusion:

  - Visuals

    - Scatterplots for continuous predictors vs. continuous outcome

    - Boxplots for categorical predictors vs. continuous outcome


  - Correlation tests (Pearson/Spearman/Kendall correlations for continuous variables)


  - Group difference tests (if relevant t-tests or ANOVA for categorical × continuous combinations)

# 3. Data Preparation and Exploration Results
Follow the approaches and reporting conventions used in the module and required in the CA Phase 2 rubric.

- Present your univariate and bivariate analysis.

- Describe preliminary patterns, direction and strength of relationships, identification of any potential nonlinear relationships


Note: predictors can be included even if the relationship appears weak, especially as control variables. Theoretical justification is acceptable when exploratory patterns are weak.



# 4. Regression Model 
If you are going to include a comparison model then call this Baseline Model.

Follow the approaches and reporting conventions used in the module and required in the CA Phase 2 rubric.


Explain:

- Which predictors were included and why

- Whether an interaction/differential effect is included



## 4.1 Model Fit and Usefulness
- Report your model for Task 1 as per examples provided. Report:

  - Adjusted R²

  - F-test

  - Coefficient estimates + significance

  - Interpretation of direction/effect size

  - Equation

  - Narrative interpretation 


## 4.2 Examination of Assumptions

- Report your model against assumptions of MLR as per examples provided:

  - Non-zero variance of predictors

  - Normality of Residuals

  - Standardized/Studentized Residuals

  - Outliers & Influential Points

  - Linearity Assumption
  
  - Homoscedasticity (Constant Variance)
  
  - Multicollinearity
  
  - Overall Diagnostic Judgment - whether assumptions and performance indicate the model is suitable


- Each assumption needs explicit interpretation.

# 4.3 Summary
- Draw a conclusion for the first model about the associated hypothesis.
